title: The Relational and Structural Dimensions of Wellbeing: A Population‐Based Latent Model of Social Conditions, Mattering, Perceived Discrimination, and Quality of Life
abstract: ABSTRACT Mattering, the experience of feeling valued and able to contribute, is a recognized determinant of wellbeing. Perceived discrimination (PD), or unfair treatment, is socially patterned and may communicate devaluation. Anti‐mattering, the subjective experience of insignificance and disregard, serves as a theoretical lens on PD, not a measured construct. Population‐level studies rarely examine mattering and PD together, their socio‐demographic patterning or associations with quality of life (QoL). In the 2024 Norwegian Quality of Life Survey ( N = 16,396), mattering, PD, and QoL were modelled as latent constructs in a structural equation model estimating direct and indirect associations with socio‐demographic predictors. Socio‐demographic factors explained 11% of the variance in mattering and 31% in PD, with the largest contributions to PD observed among younger adults and those with financial difficulties, health limitations, or immigrant backgrounds. Mattering was positively associated with QoL ( β = 0.55, β std = 0.59) and PD negatively ( β = −0.81, β std = −0.29), both p < 0.001; the model explained 61% of QoL variance. The difference in explained variance suggests that PD was more strongly patterned by the socio‐demographic factors included in the model than mattering. Welfare policy and practice therefore need to address mattering and discrimination relationally and structurally.
